# The three-node quadratic axial-bar element

This chapter develops the three-node quadratic axial-bar element as the first
higher-order extension of the two-node bar introduced earlier.

The finite element procedure developed in the previous chapters does not change.
We will still interpolate the displacement field, map the reference element to
physical space, transform derivatives through the Jacobian, construct and
integrate the element equations, assemble the global problem, and recover the
element response.

What changes is one fundamental ingredient: the **approximation space** used
within each element.

The two-node axial-bar element uses a linear displacement interpolation,

$$
  u^h\in\mathcal P_1,
$$

and therefore produces a constant strain within each element. Introducing a
third node allows the displacement approximation to be enriched to
$u^h\in\mathcal P_2$. For the regular affine element considered in this chapter,
this gives $\varepsilon^h\in\mathcal P_1$.

This change has consequences throughout the element formulation. The
strain--displacement matrix is no longer constant, strain and stress can vary
within the element, and the polynomial degrees of the stiffness and load
integrands change, affecting the quadrature required for exact integration.

At the same time, increasing the interpolation order does not imply that every
finite element solution must be quadratic. The approximation spaces are nested,

$$
  \mathcal P_0
  \subset
  \mathcal P_1
  \subset
  \mathcal P_2,
$$

so a quadratic element can also represent constant and linear displacement
fields. This connection between the approximation space and the fields that an
element can represent exactly will be one of the main themes of the chapter.

We will construct the quadratic Lagrange shape functions, specialize the
one-dimensional isoparametric formulation to a regular three-node bar, derive
its stiffness matrix and consistent distributed-load vector, and then use two
simple one-element problems to examine what the richer approximation space can
actually represent.

## Quadratic shape functions

To construct the quadratic approximation

$$
  u^h\in\mathcal P_2,
$$

consider the reference interval

$$
  -1\le\xi\le1
$$

with three interpolation nodes,

$$
  \xi_1=-1,
  \qquad
  \xi_2=0,
  \qquad
  \xi_3=1.
$$

The corresponding element displacement vector is

$$
  \mathbf u_e
  =
  \begin{bmatrix}
  u_1\\
  u_2\\
  u_3
  \end{bmatrix}.
$$

As for the two-node element, the shape functions must satisfy the nodal
interpolation conditions

$$
  N_i(\xi_j)=\delta_{ij}.
$$

Let us derive the first shape function directly from these conditions. Since
$N_1$ is quadratic, it can be expressed as the quadratic polynomial

$$
  N_1(\xi)=a+b\xi+c\xi^2.
$$

The requirements

$$
  N_1(-1)=1,
  \qquad
  N_1(0)=0,
  \qquad
  N_1(1)=0
$$

give

$$
  a=0,
  \qquad
  b=-\frac12,
  \qquad
  c=\frac12.
$$

Hence,

$$
  \boxed{
  N_1(\xi)
  =
  \frac12\xi(\xi-1).
  }
$$

Applying the same nodal conditions to the other two nodes gives

$$
  \boxed{
  N_2(\xi)=1-\xi^2
  }
$$

and

$$
  \boxed{
  N_3(\xi)
  =
  \frac12\xi(\xi+1).
  }
$$

### Using Lagrange polynomials

The direct derivation above shows how a nodal shape function is determined from
its interpolation conditions. The same functions can also be constructed
systematically using Lagrange polynomials.

For a set of interpolation nodes with reference coordinates
$\xi_1,\xi_2,\ldots,\xi_n$, the Lagrange shape function $N_i(\xi)$ is associated
with node $i$:

$$
  N_i(\xi)
  =
  \prod_{\substack{j=1\\j\ne i}}^n
  \frac{\xi-\xi_j}{\xi_i-\xi_j}.
$$

For example,

$$
  N_1(\xi)
  =
  \frac{\xi-\xi_2}{\xi_1-\xi_2}
  \frac{\xi-\xi_3}{\xi_1-\xi_3}
  =
  \frac{\xi}{-1}
  \frac{\xi-1}{-2}
  =
  \frac12\xi(\xi-1).
$$

The remaining two functions follow in the same way.

The Lagrange construction is useful because it provides a systematic procedure
for generating nodal interpolation functions once the interpolation nodes have
been specified.

The three shape functions are collected in the shape-function matrix

$$
  \mathbf N(\xi)
  =
  \begin{bmatrix}
  N_1(\xi) & N_2(\xi) & N_3(\xi)
  \end{bmatrix}.
$$

The quadratic finite element displacement field is therefore written as

$$
  \boxed{
  u^h\!\left(x(\xi)\right)
  =
  \mathbf N(\xi)\mathbf u_e.
  }
$$

The shape functions satisfy the partition-of-unity property,

$$
  N_1(\xi)+N_2(\xi)+N_3(\xi)=1.
$$

Consider a constant displacement field, for which

$$
  u_1=u_2=u_3=\bar u.
$$

The finite element interpolation then gives

$$
  u^h\!\left(x(\xi)\right)
  =
  \mathbf N(\xi)\mathbf u_e
  =
  \left(
  N_1+N_2+N_3
  \right)\bar u
  =
  \bar u.
$$

Therefore, the partition-of-unity property ensures that a constant displacement
field,

$$
  u\in\mathcal P_0,
$$

corresponding to a rigid translation of the bar, is reproduced exactly. Since
such a field has zero strain, the element does not generate spurious deformation
under rigid-body motion.

## Regular isoparametric geometry and the strain--displacement matrix

The preceding chapter showed that a three-node isoparametric geometry does not
necessarily produce a non-affine mapping. In particular, if the middle physical
node lies exactly halfway between the two end nodes, the quadratic geometry
interpolation reduces to an affine map.

We adopt that regular geometry here:

$$
  x_2=\frac{x_1+x_3}{2},
$$

with

$$
  L_e=x_3-x_1.
$$

Using

$$
  x(\xi)=\mathbf N(\xi)\mathbf x_e,
$$

the coordinate mapping becomes

$$
  x(\xi)
  =
  x_1+\frac{L_e}{2}(1+\xi),
$$

and therefore

$$
  \boxed{
  J=\frac{dx}{d\xi}=\frac{L_e}{2}.
  }
$$

The geometry is thus deliberately kept affine. The constant Jacobian allows us
to isolate the effect of increasing the displacement interpolation order: in
this regular case, $\mathbf B(\xi)$ remains linear in $\xi$. With a non-affine
geometry, $J$ would vary within the element and this simple polynomial structure
would no longer hold.

Differentiating the quadratic shape functions gives

$$
  \frac{d\mathbf N}{d\xi}
  =
  \begin{bmatrix}
  \xi-\frac12 &
  -2\xi &
  \xi+\frac12
  \end{bmatrix}.
$$

Using the derivative transformation established previously,

$$
  \mathbf B(\xi)
  =
  \frac{1}{J}
  \frac{d\mathbf N}{d\xi},
$$

we obtain

$$
  \boxed{
  \mathbf B(\xi)
  =
  \frac{2}{L_e}
  \begin{bmatrix}
  \xi-\frac12 &
  -2\xi &
  \xi+\frac12
  \end{bmatrix}.
  }
$$

Unlike the two-node bar, the strain--displacement matrix now varies within the
element.

Consequently,

$$
  \varepsilon^h\!\left(x(\xi)\right)
  =
  \mathbf B(\xi)\mathbf u_e
$$

is of degree at most one in $\xi$. Since the coordinate mapping is affine, it is
also of degree at most one in the physical coordinate $x$. For constant $E$ and
$A$, the same is true of stress and axial force.

## Element stiffness and numerical integration

The element stiffness matrix retains the same form used for the two-node bar,

$$
  \mathbf K_e
  =
  \int_{-1}^{1}
  \mathbf B(\xi)^{\mathsf T}
  EA
  \mathbf B(\xi)
  J\,d\xi.
$$

What changes is the polynomial degree of the transformed integrand.

For the regular quadratic element with constant $E$ and $A$,

$$
  \mathbf B(\xi)\in\mathcal P_1,
$$

because the derivatives of the quadratic shape functions are linear and the
Jacobian is constant. Therefore, each scalar entry of the stiffness integrand
contains a product

$$
  B_i(\xi)B_j(\xi)\in\mathcal P_2.
$$

The complete transformed scalar stiffness integrands are thus quadratic in
$\xi$.

The Gauss--Legendre rule must therefore satisfy

$$
  2n_g-1\ge2,
$$

so the minimum exact rule has

$$
  \boxed{n_g=2.}
$$

This is the first direct numerical consequence of increasing the interpolation
order. For the constant-property two-node bar, $\mathbf B$ is constant and one
Gauss point is sufficient; for the quadratic bar, $\mathbf B$ varies linearly
and two points are required.

For example,

$$
  K_{11}
  =
  \int_{-1}^{1}
  B_1(\xi)^2EAJ\,d\xi,
$$

with

$$
  B_1(\xi)
  =
  \frac{2}{L_e}
  \left(
  \xi-\frac12
  \right).
$$

The corresponding scalar integrand therefore contains the quadratic factor

$$
  \left(
  \xi-\frac12
  \right)^2.
$$

Evaluating the element integrals gives

$$
  \boxed{
  \mathbf K_e
  =
  \frac{EA}{3L_e}
  \begin{bmatrix}
  7 & -8 & 1\\
  -8 & 16 & -8\\
  1 & -8 & 7
  \end{bmatrix}.
  }
$$

Two-point Gauss--Legendre quadrature reproduces this matrix exactly.

Using fewer quadrature points is not merely less accurate in this case. With one
Gauss point, the quadratic element stiffness matrix develops an additional
zero-energy mode. This consequence of under-integration is explored in the
exercises.

## Consistent distributed loading

The consistent element load vector retains the same form,

$$
  \mathbf f_e^q
  =
  \int_{-1}^{1}
  \mathbf N(\xi)^{\mathsf T}
  q\!\left(x(\xi)\right)
  J\,d\xi.
$$

For a uniform distributed load,

$$
  q(x)=q_0,
$$

the only factor that varies with $\xi$ is the quadratic shape function. Since

$$
  N_i(\xi)\in\mathcal P_2,
$$

while $q_0$ and $J$ are constant, each scalar load-vector integrand belongs to

$$
  \mathcal P_2.
$$

The minimum exact Gauss--Legendre rule therefore again has

$$
  \boxed{n_g=2.}
$$

This provides a second direct consequence of the higher-order interpolation. For
the two-node bar with uniform loading, the corresponding load-vector integrands
are linear and one Gauss point is sufficient. For the three-node quadratic bar,
they are quadratic and require two points.

Evaluating the integrals gives

$$
  \boxed{
  \mathbf f_e^q
  =
  \frac{q_0L_e}{6}
  \begin{bmatrix}
  1\\
  4\\
  1
  \end{bmatrix}.
  }
$$

The ratio

$$
  1:4:1
$$

is not an arbitrary distribution of the total load. Each nodal contribution is
determined by the corresponding shape function through

$$
  f_{e,i}^q
  =
  q_0J
  \int_{-1}^{1}
  N_i(\xi)\,d\xi.
$$

Because the shape functions form a partition of unity, the nodal contributions
also preserve the total distributed load

$$
  \sum_{i=1}^{3} f_{e,i}^q
  =
  q_0L_e.
$$

## What the quadratic approximation can reproduce

Having derived the quadratic element formulation, we can now ask a different
question: which displacement fields can this richer approximation space
represent exactly?

The approximation space of the three-node element contains all polynomial
displacement fields up to degree two,

$$
  \mathcal P_0
  \subset
  \mathcal P_1
  \subset
  \mathcal P_2.
$$

If a displacement field belongs to one of these polynomial subspaces, the
interpolation has the capability to represent it exactly. This property is
commonly described as **polynomial completeness** or **polynomial
reproducibility**.

The three cases have a direct mechanical interpretation:

  | Displacement field | Polynomial space | Mechanical interpretation |
  | ------------------ | ---------------: | ------------------------- |
  | $u=a$              |   $\mathcal P_0$ | rigid translation         |
  | $u=a+bx$           |   $\mathcal P_1$ | constant strain           |
  | $u=a+bx+cx^2$      |   $\mathcal P_2$ | linearly varying strain   |

Thus, increasing the interpolation order enlarges the set of displacement fields
that the element can represent exactly. It does not require every finite element
solution to contain a quadratic term.

The following two one-element problems make this distinction explicit. The first
has an exact solution in the lower-order space $\mathcal P_1$; the second uses
the full quadratic space $\mathcal P_2$.

### End-force-only bar

Consider a bar of length $L$, constant $E$ and $A$, fixed at

$$
  x=0
$$

and subjected to an axial force $F$ at

$$
  x=L
$$

with no distributed load ($q(x)=0$).

The analytical solution is

$$
  u(x)
  =
  \frac{F}{EA}x.
$$

The displacement field is therefore linear.

Discretize the complete bar using one regular quadratic element,

$$
  x_1=0,
  \qquad
  x_2=\frac L2,
  \qquad
  x_3=L.
$$

The nodal force vector is

$$
  \mathbf f_e
  =
  \begin{bmatrix}
  0\\
  0\\
  F
  \end{bmatrix}.
$$

Using the quadratic-element stiffness matrix and imposing

$$
  u_1=0,
$$

yields the reduced system

$$
  \frac{EA}{3L}
  \begin{bmatrix}
  16 & -8\\
  -8 & 7
  \end{bmatrix}
  \begin{bmatrix}
  u_2\\
  u_3
  \end{bmatrix}
  =
  \begin{bmatrix}
  0\\
  F
  \end{bmatrix}.
$$

Its solution is

$$
  u_2
  =
  \frac{FL}{2EA},
  \qquad
  u_3
  =
  \frac{FL}{EA}.
$$

Substituting these values into the quadratic interpolation gives

$$
  u^h\!\left(x(\xi)\right)
  =
  \frac{FL}{EA}
  \left(
  \frac12N_2+N_3
  \right).
$$

Since

$$
  \frac12N_2+N_3
  =
  \frac{1+\xi}{2},
$$

and

$$
  x=\frac L2(1+\xi),
$$

we obtain

$$
  \boxed{
  u^h(x)=\frac{F}{EA}x.
  }
$$

For this problem, the quadratic element reproduces the linear solution exactly.
The exact displacement field belongs to $\mathcal P_1$, which is contained in
the quadratic approximation space $\mathcal P_2$.

The quadratic term is therefore not activated in this particular solution: the
element represents the lower-order linear field exactly, and the corresponding
strain is constant.

### Uniformly loaded bar

Now consider the same bar subjected to a uniform distributed axial load $q$,
with

$$
  u(0)=0
$$

and no applied axial force at

$$
  x=L.
$$

For constant $EA$,

$$
  -EA\frac{d^2u}{dx^2}=q,
$$

and the analytical solution is

$$
  \boxed{
  u(x)
  =
  \frac{q}{EA}
  \left(
  Lx-\frac{x^2}{2}
  \right),
  }
$$

which is a quadratic displacement field.

Using one regular quadratic element over the complete bar, the consistent load
vector is

$$
  \mathbf f_e^q
  =
  \frac{qL}{6}
  \begin{bmatrix}
  1\\
  4\\
  1
  \end{bmatrix}.
$$

After imposing

$$
  u_1=0,
$$

the reduced finite element equations become

$$
  \frac{EA}{3L}
  \begin{bmatrix}
  16 & -8\\
  -8 & 7
  \end{bmatrix}
  \begin{bmatrix}
  u_2\\
  u_3
  \end{bmatrix}
  =
  \frac{qL}{6}
  \begin{bmatrix}
  4\\
  1
  \end{bmatrix}.
$$

The solution is

$$
  u_2
  =
  \frac{3qL^2}{8EA},
  \qquad
  u_3
  =
  \frac{qL^2}{2EA}.
$$

Substituting these nodal values into the interpolation gives

$$
  \boxed{
  u^h(x)
  =
  \frac{q}{EA}
  \left(
  Lx-\frac{x^2}{2}
  \right).
  }
$$

One quadratic element therefore reproduces the complete analytical displacement
field exactly.

In this case,

$$
  u(x)\in\mathcal P_2,
$$

so the solution uses the full approximation space available to the element. Its
derivative is linear, and the corresponding strain varies within the element.

Together, the two examples show that the polynomial order of the element
describes its **approximation capability**, not the polynomial degree that every
particular solution must exhibit.

## Response recovery

For the quadratic element,

$$
  \varepsilon^h\!\left(x(\xi)\right)
  =
  \mathbf B(\xi)\mathbf u_e.
$$

Because $\mathbf B$ varies linearly with $\xi$, the finite element strain
generally varies within the element. For constant $E$ and $A$, the same is true
of

$$
  \sigma^h\!\left(x(\xi)\right)
  =
  E\varepsilon^h\!\left(x(\xi)\right)
$$

and

$$
  N^h\!\left(x(\xi)\right)
  =
  A\sigma^h\!\left(x(\xi)\right).
$$

Response recovery therefore no longer produces, in general, a single strain,
stress, or axial-force value for the complete element. These fields can be
evaluated at any selected position within the element.

The locations used for response evaluation should not be confused with the
quadrature points used to integrate the element equations. The same locations
may be used for both purposes, but integration and response evaluation are
different operations.

## Toward the MiniFEM implementation

The next implementation will reuse the existing isoparametric and
Gauss--Legendre framework. Rather than constructing a new finite element
workflow, we will adapt the verified two-node formulation to the quadratic
interpolation developed in this chapter.

The main element-level changes are:

- three local displacement DOFs instead of two;
- quadratic shape functions and linear shape-function derivatives;
- a strain--displacement matrix $\mathbf B(\xi)$ that varies within the element;
- two-point Gauss--Legendre quadrature for the regular constant-property
  stiffness matrix and uniform distributed load;
- response recovery for fields that can vary within the element.

The two one-element problems considered in this chapter provide reference cases
for verifying the implementation. The end-force problem must reproduce the
linear displacement field and constant strain exactly, whereas the uniformly
loaded problem must reproduce the quadratic displacement field and linear strain
exactly.

Once the quadratic element has been implemented and verified, we will move from
exact polynomial reproduction to problems that require approximation, allowing
us to introduce error measures and study convergence under mesh refinement.

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercises"}
1. Differentiate the partition-of-unity relation and verify that

   $$ \frac{dN_1}{d\xi} + \frac{dN_2}{d\xi} + \frac{dN_3}{d\xi} =
   0. $$

   Explain why this is consistent with zero strain under a rigid translation.

2. Consider a linear displacement field
   $$
   u(x)=a+bx.
   $$
   Evaluate it at the three element nodes,
   $$
   x_1,\qquad x_2=\frac{x_1+x_3}{2},\qquad x_3,
   $$
   and show directly that the quadratic interpolation reproduces the original
   field exactly.

3. Evaluate the stiffness entry

   $$
     K_{12}
   $$

   analytically and verify the corresponding entry of the closed-form element
   stiffness matrix.

4. Verify that

   $$
     \mathbf K_e
     \begin{bmatrix}
     1\\
     1\\
     1
     \end{bmatrix}
     =
     \mathbf 0.
   $$

   What physical displacement mode does this vector represent?

5. Evaluate the quadratic-element stiffness using one Gauss--Legendre point at

   $$
     \xi=0.
   $$

   Construct the resulting stiffness matrix and identify the additional
   zero-energy mode.

6. Use partition of unity to show directly that the uniform consistent load
   vector preserves the total distributed load:

   $$
     \sum_{i=1}^{3}f_{e,i}^q=q_0L_e.
   $$

7. Suppose that $q(x)$ varies linearly over the regular quadratic element.

   Determine the polynomial degree of

   $$
     N_i(\xi)q\!\left(x(\xi)\right)J
   $$

   and hence the minimum exact Gauss--Legendre rule.

   Then derive the corresponding consistent nodal load vector.

8. For the end-force-only example, substitute the finite element nodal
   displacements into

   $$
     \varepsilon^h(\xi)
     =
     \mathbf B(\xi)\mathbf u_e
   $$

   and show that the strain is constant.

   Repeat the calculation for the uniformly loaded bar and show that the strain
   varies linearly.

9. The three-node bar developed in this chapter uses the local numbering

   $$
     1 \;-\; 2 \;-\; 3,
   $$

   with node 2 at the element midpoint. In many finite element formulations,
   however, the two end nodes are numbered first and the midpoint node is
   numbered last. Relative to the numbering used in this chapter, the nodal
   positions are then reordered as

   $$
     1 \;-\; 3 \;-\; 2.
   $$

   Thus, the alternative convention assigns local nodes 1 and 2 to the element
   ends and local node 3 to the midpoint. The finite element itself has not
   changed: only the ordering of the local nodal quantities has changed. This is
   useful to understand because element matrices depend on the chosen local DOF
   ordering, even though the underlying mechanical element and its physical
   predictions remain unchanged.

   Starting from the quadratic element derived in this chapter, construct the
   element stiffness matrix for the local displacement vector

   $$
     \mathbf u_e
     =
     \begin{bmatrix}
     u_1\\
     u_2\\
     u_3
     \end{bmatrix},
   $$

   where nodes 1 and 2 are located at the two element ends and node 3 is the
   midpoint.

   Show that the resulting stiffness matrix is

   $$
     \boxed{
     \mathbf K_e
     =
     \frac{EA}{3L_e}
     \begin{bmatrix}
     7 & 1 & -8\\
     1 & 7 & -8\\
     -8 & -8 & 16
     \end{bmatrix}.
     }
   $$

   Verify this result in two different ways:

   1. Reorder the rows and columns of the stiffness matrix derived in the
      chapter. You may do this using a permutation matrix. If

      $$
        \mathbf u_e^{(123)}
        =
        \begin{bmatrix}
        u_1\\
        u_2\\
        u_3
        \end{bmatrix}
      $$

      denotes the ordering used in the chapter, with node 2 at the midpoint, and

      $$
        \mathbf u_e^{(132)}
        =
        \begin{bmatrix}
        u_1\\
        u_3\\
        u_2
        \end{bmatrix}
      $$

      denotes the ordering with the two end nodes first, then

      $$
        \mathbf u_e^{(132)}
        =
        \mathbf P\mathbf u_e^{(123)},
      $$

      with

      $$
        \mathbf P
        =
        \begin{bmatrix}
        1 & 0 & 0\\
        0 & 0 & 1\\
        0 & 1 & 0
        \end{bmatrix}.
      $$

      Use this transformation to show that

      $$
        \boxed{
        \mathbf K_e^{(132)}
        =
        \mathbf P
        \mathbf K_e^{(123)}
        \mathbf P^{\mathsf T}.
        }
      $$

      Verify that this produces the matrix given above.

   2. Verify the same result directly from the element formulation. For the new
      local ordering, first write the reordered shape-function matrix as
      $$
      \mathbf N^{(132)}(\xi)
      =
      \begin{bmatrix}
      N_1(\xi) & N_3(\xi) & N_2(\xi)
      \end{bmatrix}.
      $$
      Construct the corresponding $\mathbf B^{(132)}(\xi)$ and use
      $$
      \mathbf K_e^{(132)}
      =
      \int_{-1}^{1}
      \mathbf B^{(132)}(\xi)^{\mathsf T}
      EA
      \mathbf B^{(132)}(\xi)
      J\,d\xi
      $$
      to verify the stiffness matrix obtained by permutation.

      Explain why the two stiffness matrices have different arrangements of
      their entries but represent exactly the same finite element.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Key points to remember"}
- Increasing the interpolation order from linear to quadratic enlarges the
  approximation space from $\mathcal P_1$ to $\mathcal P_2$ without changing the
  underlying finite element procedure.

- The quadratic Lagrange shape functions satisfy the nodal interpolation
  property
  $$
  N_i(\xi_j)=\delta_{ij}
  $$
  and form a partition of unity.

- The approximation spaces are nested:
  $$
  \mathcal P_0
  \subset
  \mathcal P_1
  \subset
  \mathcal P_2.
  $$
  The quadratic element can therefore represent rigid translations, linear
  displacement fields with constant strain, and quadratic displacement fields
  with linearly varying strain.

- The polynomial order of the element describes its approximation capability. It
  does not require every finite element solution to contain terms of the highest
  available order.

- For the regular three-node element,
  $$
  J=\frac{L_e}{2},
  $$
  while $\mathbf B(\xi)$ is linear in $\xi$. For constant $E$ and $A$, strain,
  stress, and axial force can therefore vary linearly within the element.

- For constant $E$ and $A$, the stiffness integrands and the uniform-load
  integrands are quadratic in $\xi$. Two-point Gauss--Legendre quadrature is the
  minimum exact rule for both.

- The consistent nodal vector for a uniform distributed load is
  $$
  \mathbf f_e^q
  =
  \frac{q_0L_e}{6}
  \begin{bmatrix}
  1\\
  4\\
  1
  \end{bmatrix}.
  $$

- Increasing the interpolation order changes several connected parts of the
  element formulation: it enriches the approximation space, changes
  $\mathbf B(\xi)$ and the variation of the recovered fields within the element,
  increases the polynomial degree of the element integrands, and can therefore
  increase the quadrature order required for exact integration.
:::
